title: Authority Over Disease, Storm, and Demons
summary: Coming down from the mountain, Jesus cleanses a leper with a touch, heals a centurion's servant with a word from a distance, and lifts Peter's mother-in-law from a fever, and Matthew sees in the day's healings Isaiah's servant who carries our diseases. Two would-be followers learn what following him costs. He calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee and frees two demon-possessed men on the far shore, whose town then asks him to leave.
story:
Matthew has just finished the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5 to 7), which ended with the crowds astonished that Jesus taught as one who had authority. Chapters 8 and 9 now show that authority in action: the words of the mountain become deeds in the towns and on the lake. Matthew frames the whole unit with two nearly identical summaries of Jesus teaching, preaching, and healing (4:23 and 9:35), so that chapters 5 to 7 give the Messiah's word and chapters 8 and 9 the Messiah's work. When John the Baptist later asks from prison whether Jesus is the one to come, Jesus answers by listing deeds that these two chapters have already shown: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised (11:4-5).

The order of the first stories is telling. The first people helped are a leper, a Gentile soldier's servant, and a woman, all on the edges of religious life as it was usually measured. The chapter also begins threads that run to the end of the Gospel. A pagan officer shows greater faith than Jesus has found in Israel, and Jesus pictures many coming from east and west to the banquet of the kingdom, anticipating the commission to make disciples of all nations (28:19). The word follow runs through the chapter, from the crowds who follow him down the mountain (verse 1) to the disciples who follow him into a boat and a storm (verse 23). And at the end a Gentile town, faced with two men restored and a herd lost, would rather Jesus went away, a first sign of the refusal that will grow in the chapters ahead.
historical:
These events take place in Galilee, which in Jesus' adult life was ruled by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, as tetrarch (a subordinate ruler under Rome) from 4 BC to AD 39. Capernaum, the town Matthew calls Jesus' own (4:13, 9:1), was a fishing and farming village on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, near the border with the territory of Antipas's brother Philip to the east. In 1968 the Franciscan archaeologists Virgilio Corbo and Stanislao Loffreda began nearly twenty seasons of excavation there. Under a fifth-century octagonal church about thirty meters south of the later limestone synagogue they found a first-century house whose main room had been set apart and replastered, with Christian graffiti invoking Jesus and Peter scratched into its walls, and a fourth-century house church built around it. A description attributed to the pilgrim Egeria in the late fourth century says the house of Peter at Capernaum had been made into a church with its walls still standing. The identification cannot be proved, but it is one of the oldest continuous Christian memories attached to a place in Galilee, and a modern church was built over the site in 1990.

The centurion was an officer who commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers. Since Galilee was not under direct Roman administration until AD 44, he most likely served in Antipas's forces, which were organized on Roman lines and often recruited from non-Jews in the region; Josephus describes Antipas's army being destroyed by the Nabatean king Aretas IV around AD 36 (Antiquities 18.113-115). Either way he was a Gentile. Luke tells the same healing (Luke 7:1-10) and adds that Jewish elders spoke for him because he loved the nation and had built their synagogue.

Leprosy in the Bible (Hebrew tsara‘at, Greek lepra) covers a range of skin diseases, and even mold on cloth or walls (Leviticus 13 and 14), not only what is now called Hansen's disease. Hansen's disease did exist in the land in this period: in 2000 Shimon Gibson, Boaz Zissu, and James Tabor excavated a first-century tomb in the Hinnom Valley at Jerusalem, the traditional Akeldama, and DNA analysis published in 2009 found Mycobacterium leprae in the shrouded remains of a man buried there, the earliest securely dated case of leprosy confirmed by DNA. Jewish practice kept such sufferers apart. The Law required the person to live outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45-46), the Temple Scroll from Qumran sets aside places east of the city for lepers and others with discharges (11Q19 46:16-18), the Mishnah says lepers are sent out of walled cities (m. Kelim 1:7), and Josephus says Moses forbade lepers to stay in a town or live in a village (Against Apion 1.281).

The far shore of the lake lay in the region of the Decapolis, a league of Greek cities that Pompey had freed from Jewish rule in 63 BC. Gadara, modern Umm Qais, stood on a height about six miles southeast of the lake, and its territory probably reached the shore. It was a proud center of Greek culture; the Cynic satirist Menippus, the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus, and the poet Meleager all came from it. Mark and Luke name the region after Gerasa, modern Jerash, more than thirty miles away, and in the third century Origen preferred Gergesa, an old town on the shore (Commentary on John 6.41). In 1970 road builders on the eastern shore uncovered remains at Kursi, where Vassilios Tzaferis excavated a large Byzantine monastery and a chapel on the slope above it, evidently marking the traditional site of this miracle; many connect Kursi with Origen's Gergesa. The manuscripts of all three Gospels vary among the names (see text).
cultural:
Under Leviticus 13 and 14 a person with such a disease was ritually unclean, had to tear his clothes, cover his upper lip, and cry ‘Unclean, unclean’, and could return to community life only after a priest inspected him and the prescribed offerings were made: two birds, then on the eighth day lambs, flour, and oil (Leviticus 14:1-32). Impurity was not sin, and it barred a person chiefly from the sanctuary and from sacred food, but tsara‘at was the one impurity that also removed a person from ordinary society. Cure was thought to be God's work alone. When the king of Aram sent Naaman to be healed, the king of Israel tore his clothes and asked whether he was God, to kill and to make alive (2 Kings 5:7), and Aaron described Miriam's leprosy as being like a stillborn child (Numbers 12:12). To touch a leper was to share his uncleanness. Jesus reverses the flow: his touch does not make him unclean, it makes the leper clean. He then sends the man to the priest, honoring the law of Moses and giving the priests testimony of what had happened.

A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile's house. Peter tells Cornelius, another centurion, that it is unlawful for a Jew to associate with or visit a foreigner (Acts 10:28), and the Mishnah says that the dwelling places of Gentiles are unclean (m. Oholot 18:7). The centurion seems to know this and spares Jesus the problem, asking only for a word. His reasoning comes from military life: authority flows downward through a chain of command, and an order given is an order done. He does not ask Jesus to come; he recognizes that Jesus' word has the same kind of reach.

Fever was feared as a killer and in the Law is named among the afflictions of the covenant curse (Leviticus 26:16, Deuteronomy 28:22). Peter's mother-in-law, once healed, rises and serves, the ordinary work of hospitality, which shows the cure was complete. That Peter had a wife is confirmed by Paul, who says Cephas took a believing wife with him on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5). The crowds come ‘when evening came’; Mark places this at the end of a Sabbath (Mark 1:21, 32), when carrying the sick was again permitted.

Burying one's father was among the most sacred duties in Jewish life, a way of honoring father and mother (Exodus 20:12). The Mishnah exempts a man whose dead lies before him from reciting the Shema, the daily confession of faith (m. Berakhot 3:1), and Tobit's father asks his son to bury him properly (Tobit 4:3). Only the high priest and a Nazirite under a vow were forbidden to attend even a parent's burial (Leviticus 21:10-11, Numbers 6:6-7), for the sake of their holiness to God. When Elisha asked to kiss his parents goodbye before following Elijah, he was allowed (1 Kings 19:19-21). Jesus' reply goes further than any of these, which is why it has shocked readers ever since. First-century Jews in Judea often practiced secondary burial: the body was laid in a tomb, and about a year later a son gathered the bones into an ossuary. Byron McCane (Harvard Theological Review, 1990) argued that the man may have been asking to wait until that reburial; Kenneth Bailey (Through Peasant Eyes, 1980), drawing on Middle Eastern idiom, argued that the father was probably still alive and the request meant waiting until he died. On any reading, Jesus claims a loyalty that outranks the most honored family duty.

The lake is about thirteen miles long and seven or eight miles wide, lies some seven hundred feet below sea level, and is ringed by hills through which cold winds can drop suddenly and raise dangerous waves. A first-century fishing boat found in the mud near Kibbutz Ginosar in 1986 shows the kind of vessel involved: about 8.3 meters (27 feet) long, with room for a crew and passengers. Sleeping through a storm could look like either exhaustion or complete trust. Pigs, forbidden as food under Leviticus 11:7, mark the far shore as Gentile country, and the Mishnah forbids Jews to raise them anywhere (m. Bava Kamma 7:7). Tombs, often caves cut in the hillside, were places of corpse impurity (Numbers 19:11-16) and, in popular belief, haunts of spirits.
literary:
Matthew arranges chapters 8 and 9 as nine miracle stories (ten miracles, since 9:18-26 contains two) in three groups of three, separated by two short sections about discipleship. The first group (8:1-17: leper, centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law) ends with a summary and a fulfillment quotation from Isaiah. Then comes a scene on the cost of following (8:18-22). The second group follows (the storm, the demoniacs, and the paralytic in 9:1-8), then a second interlude about following and feasting (9:9-17), and a third group (9:18-34). This is not Mark's order; Matthew has gathered stories that Mark spreads across 1:29-5:43 and arranged them by theme.

Matthew also tells these stories more briefly than Mark and Luke, trimming vivid detail and keeping the dialogue. Heinz Joachim Held (in Tradition and Interpretation in Matthew, English 1963) showed that this compression is purposeful: Matthew turns the miracle stories into conversations about faith and about who Jesus is. Two words bind the chapter. One is faith: the centurion's great faith (verse 10), ‘as you have believed’ (verse 13), and the disciples' little faith (verse 26). The other is following (akoloutheō), which appears in verses 1, 10, 19, 22, and 23. There is also a quiet pattern in how people address Jesus. The scribe calls him Teacher (verse 19), the way outsiders and opponents address him in Matthew; the disciple (verse 21), the leper (verse 2), the centurion (verses 6 and 8), and the frightened disciples (verse 25) call him Lord.

Günther Bornkamm's essay on the stilling of the storm (1948, English 1963) became a founding study of redaction criticism, the study of how each evangelist shaped his sources. He noticed that Matthew places the storm immediately after the sayings on the cost of following, that he alone says the disciples ‘followed Him’ into the boat, and that he moves Jesus' rebuke of their little faith before the miracle, where Mark puts it after. The boat becomes a picture of discipleship under pressure, and Matthew calls the storm a seismos megas, a great shaking, the word he uses elsewhere for earthquakes (24:7, 27:54, 28:2). The scene also echoes Jonah: a storm on the sea, a sleeping man, terrified sailors who cry that they are perishing, a sudden calm, and men filled with awe (Jonah 1:4-16). Later Jesus will say that something greater than Jonah is here (12:41). Finally, Matthew has two demoniacs where Mark 5 and Luke 8 have one, a pattern he repeats with two blind men in 9:27 and 20:30 where Mark has one.

outline.t: A leper is cleansed by a touch
The centurion's faith and the servant healed from a distance
Peter's mother-in-law and many others healed
Two demon-possessed men freed in Gadarene country

doctrines.note: The chapter answers the disciples' question in verse 27, “What kind of man is this?” He heals by touch and by word, and Matthew reads the day's healings through Isaiah's servant who “took on our infirmities and carried our diseases” (verse 17, from Isaiah 53:4). He calls himself the Son of Man for the first time in Matthew (verse 20), and the demons call him Son of God (verse 29).

The healings are signs that God's reign has arrived and is pushing back disease, chaos, and evil powers. Jesus pictures the kingdom as the promised banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (verse 11, compare Isaiah 25:6-8) and warns that those who assume a seat at the table may find themselves outside (verse 12).

Faith here is trust in Jesus' power and willingness. The leper is sure Jesus can and asks whether he will (verse 2); the centurion believes a word from a distance is enough (verse 8). The disciples in the storm are called ‘of little faith’, not faithless: they turn to Jesus, but fear shows they have not grasped who is in the boat.

The demons recognize Jesus as Son of God and know that a time of judgment is appointed for them (verse 29). They are real, many, and destructive, but they cannot act without his word, and a single ‘Go’ sends them out (verse 32). Scripture presents such powers as already under the authority of the one who has come to bind them (12:28-29).

A Gentile's faith surpasses what Jesus has found in Israel, and Jesus foresees many coming from east and west (verse 11), language the prophets used for the gathering of God's scattered people and for the nations streaming to Zion. Jesus also crosses to Gentile land. The chapter anticipates the mission to all nations that closes the Gospel (28:19).

words.note: Katharizō, to cleanse or make clean. It occurs about thirty-one times in the New Testament, seven in Matthew, and it is the Greek Old Testament's word for the priest declaring a person clean (Leviticus 13 and 14). In verses 2 and 3 it appears three times and carries both senses at once: the leper asks to be made clean, not merely cured, and Jesus answers in the same word. The cleansing of lepers is one of the signs Jesus names to John (11:5), and he gives the Twelve authority to do it (10:8).

Pais, child, boy, or servant. It occurs twenty-four times in the New Testament, eight in Matthew, with a range BDAG sets out from a young person, son or daughter, to a servant or slave of any age. Matthew uses pais here (verses 6, 8, 13); Luke's version calls the man a slave (doulos, Luke 7:2) as well as pais, and the similar story in John 4:46-54 has a son. Matthew also uses pais for Isaiah's servant (12:18). Theodore Jennings and Tat-siong Benny Liew (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2004) argued that the word implies a sexual relationship between the officer and the young man; Denis Saddington (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2006), an expert on the Roman army, replied that the word and the military setting point to a valued servant, which is the reading of most commentators.

Hikanos, sufficient, fit, worthy. It occurs about thirty-nine times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke and Acts, often meaning large or considerable (a great crowd, a long time). In verse 8 it means qualified or fit: ‘I am not fit that you should come under my roof’. John the Baptist uses the same word of himself (3:11, ‘not worthy to carry His sandals’), and Paul says he is not fit to be called an apostle (1 Corinthians 15:9). The officer who commands others knows he has no standing before this Lord, and his words entered the church's liturgy.

Bastazō, to carry, bear, or take up a burden. It occurs about twenty-seven times in the New Testament: carrying a jar or sandals, bearing a cross (John 19:17), bearing one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2). In verse 17 Matthew uses it to render the Hebrew of Isaiah 53:4, which speaks of the servant bearing our sicknesses (holi) and carrying our pains, where the Greek Old Testament had spiritualized the line to speak of sins. Matthew's own translation keeps the physical sense: in healing the sick, Jesus takes up their burden.

Akoloutheō, to follow. It occurs about ninety times in the New Testament, twenty-five in Matthew and almost always in the Gospels, where it can mean simply walking behind someone or, as a technical term, becoming a disciple. It appears five times in this chapter (verses 1, 10, 19, 22, 23) and moves from the one sense to the other: crowds follow, a scribe offers to follow, Jesus commands ‘Follow Me’, and the disciples follow him into a boat that is about to be swamped.

Seismos, a shaking, usually an earthquake. It occurs fourteen times in the New Testament, seven in Revelation and four in Matthew. Matthew alone uses it for the storm (verse 24); elsewhere in his Gospel it marks the earthquakes of the last days (24:7), of Jesus' death (27:54), and of the resurrection morning (28:2). The choice suggests that the storm is more than weather, a shaking of the kind that accompanies God's acts in history.

Oligopistos, of little faith. It occurs five times in the New Testament, four times in Matthew (6:30, 8:26, 14:31, 16:8) and once in Luke (12:28), always on Jesus' lips and always to disciples; the noun oligopistia appears in 17:20. It describes trust that is real but too small for the situation, which is a gentler diagnosis than Mark's ‘Do you still have no faith?’ (Mark 4:40).

Basanizō, to torment, torture, or harass. It occurs about twelve times in the New Testament: the centurion's servant is ‘in terrible agony’ (verse 6), the boat in 14:24 is buffeted by waves, and in Revelation it is used for judgment (Revelation 14:10, 20:10). In verse 29 the demons fear being tormented ‘before the appointed time’, which assumes the Jewish expectation, found in 1 Enoch and Jubilees, that evil spirits are allowed to act until a fixed day of judgment. They recognize that in Jesus that judgment has arrived early.

christ:
Matthew shows Jesus doing what the Old Testament says only God does. Cleansing a leper was, in the words of Israel's king, the work of the God who kills and makes alive (2 Kings 5:7), and Jesus does it with a touch and ‘I am willing’. The centurion recognizes that Jesus' word carries authority over sickness the way a commander's word carries authority over soldiers, and the Psalms say that God sent his word and healed them (Psalm 107:20). In the same psalm the LORD calms the storm: “He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29). Here Jesus rebukes the winds and the sea, and the disciples ask the question the whole Gospel answers: what kind of man is this?

Matthew reads the healings through Isaiah 53, the song of the suffering servant. The line he quotes, “He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases” (verse 17), comes from a passage that goes on to speak of the servant pierced for transgressions and bearing iniquity (Isaiah 53:5-6, 11-12). Matthew applies it first to healing, and the reader who continues to the cross will see where that carrying leads. Some Jewish tradition also read Isaiah 53:4 of the Messiah: in a playful passage of the Babylonian Talmud in which different schools give the Messiah names, one calls him the leper and another the sick one, citing this verse (b. Sanhedrin 98b).

Jesus' self-description in verse 20 is the first time Matthew uses the title Son of Man, which draws on Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives from the Ancient of Days an everlasting kingdom and the service of all peoples. Here the one who will receive all authority (28:18) has nowhere to lay his head. The banquet saying (verses 11 and 12) takes up the prophets' promise of a feast for all peoples on God's mountain (Isaiah 25:6-8) and their pictures of people gathered from east and west (Psalm 107:3, Isaiah 43:5-6, Malachi 1:11), and it puts Jesus at the center as the one whose word decides who sits at the table. The demons call him Son of God and know he is their judge. The chapter shows who Jesus is: God's servant who carries human burdens, the Lord of wind and sea, and the Son of Man who shares the homelessness of the poor on his way to receive the kingdom.
interpretation:
The centurion's words have been spoken in worship more often than almost any other sentence in the Gospels. In the Roman Mass, since the Middle Ages, the people say before communion, in words adapted from verse 8, that they are not worthy that the Lord should come under their roof, but only say the word and their soul shall be healed; the English translation of the Roman Missal introduced in 2011 restored the phrase ‘under my roof’, which the 1973 translation had dropped. Augustine (Sermon 62) held the centurion up as a model of humility: by counting himself unworthy to receive Christ under his roof, he received him into his heart. In his Harmony of the Gospels (2.20) Augustine explained that Matthew reports as the centurion's own words what Luke says was carried by messengers, as one speaks of approaching someone through intermediaries, and he explained the two demoniacs (2.24) by suggesting that one of them was better known in the region, so that Mark and Luke named only him. On the ruler's daughter in the next chapter he used the same principle (2.28).

The storm quickly became a picture of the church. Tertullian (On Baptism 12, around 200) wrote that the little ship was a figure of the church, tossed in the sea of the world by the waves of persecution and temptation while the Lord seems to sleep, until the prayers of the saints rouse him to calm it. Origen (Commentary on John 6.41) rejected both Gerasa and Gadara as too far from the lake and preferred Gergesa, and later manuscripts followed him. In the Byzantine church the chapter is read on Sundays after Pentecost: the healing of the centurion's servant on the fourth, the demoniacs on the fifth, and in the next chapter the paralytic on the sixth and the two blind men on the seventh; Theophylact of Ohrid's eleventh-century commentary on Matthew preserves the Greek tradition of reading them.

Modern study of the Gospels turned on this chapter. Bornkamm's 1948 essay on the storm, with Held's study of Matthew's miracle stories, launched redaction criticism. Martin Hengel's Nachfolge und Charisma (1968; English, The Charismatic Leader and His Followers, 1981) took ‘let the dead bury their own dead’ as its starting point and argued that no rabbi of the time made such a demand, so that Jesus' call to follow him resembled a prophet's or charismatic leader's authority rather than a teacher's. Dale Allison (Irish Biblical Studies, 1989) argued that those who come ‘from east and west’ in verse 11 were originally the scattered Jews of the diaspora rather than Gentiles, as in the Old Testament texts it echoes, while most commentators read Matthew's setting, after a Gentile's faith, as pointing to the nations.

Verse 17 has had a contested life in modern Christianity. Leaders of the nineteenth-century divine-healing movement, such as A. B. Simpson (The Gospel of Healing), and later Pentecostal teachers such as F. F. Bosworth (Christ the Healer, 1924) taught that bodily healing is provided in the atonement and may be claimed by faith, citing this verse. B. B. Warfield (Counterfeit Miracles, 1918) and many others replied that Matthew applies Isaiah to Jesus' earthly healings as signs of the kingdom, not as a promise that believers will now be spared all sickness. In art, Paolo Veronese painted Christ and the Centurion several times in the 1570s (one version is in the Prado), and Rembrandt's only seascape, The Storm on the Sea of Galilee (1633), showing the boat heeling in a wave while terrified disciples wake Jesus, hung in the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston until it was stolen in 1990; it has never been recovered.
text:
The place name in verse 28 is the best-known difficulty, and it varies in all three Gospels. In Matthew the best manuscripts, led by Codex Vaticanus and supported by the Syriac versions, read ‘Gadarenes’, which modern editions and versions print; the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus has ‘Gazarenes’, another spelling of the same name. A corrector of Sinaiticus, Codex Washingtonianus, and most later Greek manuscripts read ‘Gergesenes’, the name Origen preferred, and that is the reading of the Textus Receptus and so of the King James Version, which has ‘Gergesenes’ here but ‘Gadarenes’ in Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26. Much of the Latin tradition reads ‘Gerasenes’, as the best text of Mark and Luke does. Scribes plainly tried to correct the geography or to bring the Gospels into line, and each Gospel's best reading probably names the district by a different city.

In verse 10 the earliest manuscripts read ‘with no one in Israel have I found such faith’; the Byzantine text followed by the King James Version reads ‘not even in Israel’ (‘no, not in Israel’), probably from Luke 7:9. At the end of verse 13 Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Ephraemi, and a few other witnesses add a sentence saying that the centurion returned to his house in that hour and found the servant well, an addition shaped by Luke 7:10 that no modern edition prints. In verse 25 later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add ‘his disciples’ as the subject and ‘us’ after ‘save’. In verse 17 the difference is not between manuscripts but between Matthew and the Greek Old Testament: Matthew renders the Hebrew of Isaiah 53:4 directly rather than following the Septuagint, which speaks of bearing our sins. English versions also differ on pais in verses 6, 8, and 13 (‘servant’ in most, ‘boy’ in some, ‘young man’ in others) and on the man's condition in verse 6 (‘paralyzed’, BSB and ESV; ‘sick of the palsy’, KJV).

teach.big: Jesus' authority, the same authority that taught on the mountain, cleanses the unclean, heals at a word, calms the storm, and frees the oppressed, and it calls for a faith that trusts his word and a following that costs everything.

outline.t: Jesus is both able and willing: he touches the untouchable and makes him clean, and he honors the Law by sending the man to the priest.
Great faith trusts Jesus' word without needing his presence, and it can be found where insiders least expect it; belonging to the kingdom is not inherited.
In healing the sick Jesus fulfills Isaiah's servant, taking up human burdens on the way to bearing sin at the cross.
Following Jesus means sharing his homelessness and putting his call above even the most sacred family duty; he asks for loyalty, not admiration.
Disciples who follow Jesus still meet storms; little faith is fear that forgets who is in the boat, and the answer is to look again at who he is.
Jesus frees people no one else could help, and some would rather lose him than lose what his coming costs them.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first uses verse 17 to promise that every believer who has enough faith will be healed now. Matthew applies Isaiah to Jesus' earthly ministry as a sign that the kingdom has come, and the same Gospel shows faithful people suffering (5:10-12, 10:16-22); teach healing as a foretaste of the resurrection, not a guarantee. The second turns the leper's story into a picture of Jesus overthrowing the Law. He sends the man to the priest with the offering Moses commanded; what is new is the direction of contagion, not contempt for purity. The third reads verses 11 and 12 as God's rejection of the Jewish people. Jesus is speaking as a Jew to Jews, all his first disciples were Jews, and the warning is against presumption, the same warning John the Baptist gave (3:9); it applies with equal force to Christians who assume their place.

The fourth softens verse 22 until it says nothing, or hardens it into permission to neglect aging parents. Jesus elsewhere condemns those who evade care for father and mother (15:3-6); the saying is about the absolute priority of his call, spoken to a particular man at a particular moment. The fifth treats the storm as a promise that Jesus will always calm our circumstances if we have faith. Matthew's point is who Jesus is and what little faith looks like; many faithful people have gone down in storms. The sixth uses the Gadarene story to diagnose mental illness as demonic, or to dismiss the Gospels as mistaken; the Gospels distinguish illness from possession (4:24), and the text licenses no one to diagnose a neighbor.
teach.pastoral: People with chronic or stigmatized illness, and those who have been treated as untouchable because of disease, disability, or disfigurement, will hear the leper's question, if you are willing, as their own. Let Jesus' touch and his ‘I am willing’ speak before any application. The saying about burying the dead will press on the grieving and on those caring for dying parents; make clear that Jesus is not scorning grief or family love, and that caring for parents is part of obedience (15:4-6). Those living with anxiety or panic may hear ‘You of little faith’ as a rebuke that adds shame to fear; note that Jesus speaks to people who have come to him, that he calms the storm anyway, and that little faith is still faith. Families living with severe mental illness will hear the description of the two men among the tombs; teach with compassion, without suggesting that illness is spiritual failure, and keep a path to real help visible (a doctor, a counselor, a crisis line) alongside the church's prayer.

hard.q: Matthew has two demoniacs and names Gadara; Mark and Luke have one man and name Gerasa. Do the Gospels contradict each other?
hard.a:
The objection is straightforward. Mark 5:1-20 and Luke 8:26-39 tell of one man, with a name (Legion), a long conversation, and a commission to go home and tell; Matthew tells of two men in seven verses. The place differs too, and the manuscripts of all three Gospels show scribes trying to fix it. Matthew has the same doubling elsewhere: two blind men at Jericho (20:30) where Mark has one, Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46), and two blind men in 9:27, and he has two animals at the triumphal entry (21:2-7) where the others have one. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) treated such differences as signs of legend, and many critical scholars today conclude that Matthew, who used Mark, deliberately doubled the figures, whether to supply the two witnesses the Law requires (Deuteronomy 19:15), to heighten the scene, or to make up for Mark's first exorcism in the Capernaum synagogue (Mark 1:23-28), which Matthew omits. On this view Matthew is theological storytelling, not a revised report.

Responses fall into several groups. The oldest, Augustine's (Harmony of the Gospels 2.24), is that there were two men and that Mark and Luke tell only of the one who was better known or who spoke, which is not a contradiction, since they do not say there was only one; many later harmonizers and conservative commentators have followed him. On the place, the names need not conflict: Gadara was the city whose territory probably reached the shore, Gerasa the best-known city of the region, and Gergesa, if it is Kursi, the village on the spot, so each writer may have named the district from a different point of reference. Others, including scholars who hold a high view of Scripture, grant that Matthew shaped his material deliberately and argue that the Gospels' standard of accuracy was that of ancient biography, which allowed abbreviation, compression, and arrangement without deceit; on this view the doubling may reflect Matthew's concern for two witnesses without implying a false report. Readers who share a high view of Scripture differ over which explanation is best, and skeptical readers find none of them convincing. The story's point is the same in all three Gospels: people destroyed by forces beyond them are freed by Jesus' word, and a town asks him to leave.

hard.q: Does Jesus teach that Gentiles will replace Israel when he says the sons of the kingdom will be thrown out?
hard.a:
The objection is serious because of how the verse has been used. For centuries Christian preachers read verses 11 and 12 as God's rejection of the Jewish people and their replacement by a Gentile church, a reading that fed contempt for Jews and, in the worst periods, violence against them. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine (The Misunderstood Jew, 2006) have warned that such readings misrepresent both Jesus and first-century Judaism, and many historians think Matthew's harsh language reflects the bitter separation between his church and the synagogue after AD 70 as much as the words of Jesus. The phrase ‘the sons of the kingdom’ sounds like a blanket description of Israel, and ‘outer darkness’ and ‘weeping and gnashing of teeth’, a phrase Matthew uses six times (8:12, 13:42, 13:50, 22:13, 24:51, 25:30), is his strongest language of final exclusion.

Responses begin with the context. Jesus is a Jew speaking to Jews; the centurion is praised, but the disciples who will sit on twelve thrones (19:28) are all Israelites, and Jesus has just sent a Jewish leper to the priest. The warning is against presumption, that descent from Abraham guarantees a place, which John the Baptist had already made (3:9) and which the prophets made before him (Amos 3:2, Jeremiah 7:4). The same Gospel uses ‘sons of the kingdom’ in 13:38 for the good seed, the true disciples, so the phrase names a status that can be claimed falsely, not an ethnic group. Dale Allison (1989) argued that the many from east and west were originally diaspora Jews, so that the saying contrasted privileged and marginal Israelites; most commentators, including Ulrich Luz, think Matthew applies it to Gentiles, but as additions to the patriarchs' table, not replacements of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Christians differ on how Israel and the church relate: some traditions stress continuity, the church as the renewed Israel into which Gentiles are grafted (Romans 11:17-24), and others stress God's continuing purpose for ethnic Israel (Romans 11:25-29). Paul's own conclusion, that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), stands against any reading of this verse that treats the Jewish people as cast off, and the warning of verse 12 falls first on anyone, Jew or Gentile, who assumes a place at the table.

observe: What does the leper say to Jesus, and what three things does Jesus do in response (verses 2 to 4)?
How does the centurion explain why a word from Jesus is enough, and what does Jesus say about his faith?
What do the disciples say when they wake Jesus, what does he say to them, and what do they ask afterward?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus touched the leper rather than healing him with a word, and why did he send him to the priest?
What does Matthew mean by applying Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus' healings, and how does it connect with the cross?
Why do you think the townspeople begged Jesus to leave, when two of their neighbors had been freed?
apply: The leper was sure Jesus could, but unsure he would. Which do you find harder to believe about God, and why?
Jesus' call outranked even the duty of burying a father. What claims on your time and loyalty compete with following him, and how do you tell the difference between a duty and an excuse?
Think of a storm you are in now. What would it look like to bring it to Jesus with the faith you have, even if it is little?
